ennis2015.title: Discount Window Lending: Policy Trade-offs and the 1985 BoNY Computer Failure
ennis2015.author: Huberto M. Ennis and David A. Price
ennis2015.venue: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Economic Brief EB15-05
ennis2015.quote: On November 21, 1985, the Bank of New York (BoNY) suffered a software failure that left it unable to redeliver securities it had received from other institutions as an intermediary. The result of the failure was that the bank sought and received $22.6 billion in discount window lending from the New York Fed, a record-setting amount. … In 1985, BoNY was one of the four institutions responsible for clearing most Treasury securities trades for major Wall Street brokers. These transactions were carried out through an electronic securities transfer system operated by the Fed called Fedwire. … The Fed operated the system on a delivery-versus-payment basis. In such a system, when a clearing agent receives securities from the selling side of a transaction, the system automatically debits funds from the agent's reserve account to pay the party delivering the securities; throughout the day, this process can result in the clearing agent accumulating reserve account overdrafts (known as daylight overdrafts). … Normally, BoNY would use information in the database to direct the New York Fed where to send the securities that BoNY was receiving; because BoNY was unable to do so, it was not receiving any payments to offset the debits that the New York Fed was taking out of its account. … A flaw in the software caused it to fail when it processed 32,000 transactions, a volume it had reached the previous day. BoNY's database of accounts and transactions had been damaged, making recovery highly difficult. … As transactions flowed in for which BoNY could not make redelivery, the bank rapidly accumulated daylight overdrafts with the New York Fed, totaling more than $20 billion by 2:15 p.m. … By 8:30 p.m., with BoNY finally processing a trickle of its clearing transactions, its overdraft was nearly $30 billion. The New York Fed extended the business hours of Fedwire; the securities wire would remain open until 1:30 a.m. and the funds wire until 2:15 a.m. … At the closing time of the funds wire, BoNY obtained a discount window loan of $22.6 billion, 150 percent of the bank's assets and more than three times the size of the peak borrowing of Continental Illinois the previous year. (The loan was fully secured by the customers' Treasury securities in addition to the assets of the bank itself.) Because BoNY miscalculated its position when Fedwire closed at 2:15 a.m., its reserve account was overdrawn by a further $1 billion, so the total credit it received from the New York Fed was $23.6 billion. … On the following day, November 22, BoNY was still not fully operational and accumulated an additional overdraft of $2 billion by 11 a.m. The New York Fed then stopped accepting securities transfers for BoNY's account for approximately an hour and a half. … Both Volcker and Corrigan expressed support for such a policy following the BoNY episode. Under the rules of the discount window at that time, the interest rate of 7.5 percent paid by BoNY was actually less than the prevailing federal funds rate. (BoNY did pay a penalty rate on its $1 billion overdraft.) Today, as the result of a policy change in 2003, the Fed charges a penalty rate for discount window lending in general.

BoNY normally used the damaged database to tell the New York Fed where to forward arriving securities
the software failed at 32,000 transactions
the database of accounts and transactions was damaged
$22.6 billion discount window loan, $23.6 billion total credit

lacker2003.title: Payment System Disruptions and the Federal Reserve Following September 11, 2001
lacker2003.author: Jeffrey M. Lacker
lacker2003.venue: Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond Working Paper 03-16
lacker2003.quote: Faulty software prevented BoNY from sending securities to counterparties at times during the day on Thursday, November 21. This also prevented them from collecting the offsetting payments on those securities. (The exchange of a security and an offsetting payment are simultaneous under Fedwire's delivery-versus-payment regime.) They continued to receive securities and funds transfers but the inability to send securities meant that they ran up an overdraft during the day. Although the Fedwire securities system was kept open late to provide time to attempt to solve the problem, these attempts were unsuccessful and the securities system was closed at 1:30 a.m. on Friday morning and the funds system was closed at 2:15 a.m. BoNY borrowed $700 million from the private sector after midnight, but ended the day overdrawn by $23.6 billion. … [footnote 29] BoNY's initial estimate of its position at 2:15 was the basis for the discount window loan of $22.6 billion, but that estimate was incorrect and BoNY incurred an additional $1 billion in the form of an overnight overdraft. See the prepared statement of E. Gerald Corrigan, p. 6 … At the time of the most recent call report on September 30, 1985, BoNY had total assets of $15.9 billion. Under the terms of the special loan agreement covering the advance, negotiated earlier on Thursday, the advance was secured by all of the assets of the bank as well as all of the customer securities they were empowered to pledge. The Federal Reserve Bank of New York estimated the book value of the assets securing the advance at $36 billion.
supports: securities kept arriving while BoNY could not send
delivery-versus-payment makes the debit automatic and simultaneous
funds wire closed 2:15 a.m.; $23.6 billion overdrawn
BoNY total assets $15.9 billion at the 30 September 1985 call report
collateral book value estimated at $36 billion

berry1985.title: Computer Snarled N.Y. Bank — $32 Billion Overdraft Resulted From Snafu (Washington Post, 13 December 1985, p. D7), reposted in RISKS Digest Volume 1 Issue 31
berry1985.author: John M. Berry
berry1985.quote: On Wednesday, Nov. 20, transactions involving more than 32,000 different government securities issues poured into the Bank of New York, one of the largest processors of such deals on behalf of others. The bank's computer system was supposed to be able to cope with up to 36,000 issues, but a programming glitch developed and, unknown to anyone, the computer began to "corrupt" the transactions and make it impossible for the bank to keep them straight. Because of the computer system breakdown, the bank could not instruct New York Fed where to send the securities arriving at the Fed on behalf of the bank's clients, and therefore could not get paid for them. The New York Fed was automatically taking money out of the Bank of New York's cash account to pay the sellers for the incoming securities … By Thursday evening … the bank had a $32 billion overdraft on its cash account at the New York Federal Reserve Bank. The bank's computer specialists finally came up with a "patch" for its computer program — a process described yesterday by its chairman, J. Carter Bacot, as the electronic equivalent of patching a tire — that allowed it to begin to clear some of the backlog. But just after midnight, the patch failed too … The Fed kept both its nationwide wires for securities and cash transactions open in the early hours of Friday morning. When the patch failed, the Bank of New York was still able to borrow $700 million from other banks. The rest was covered by a $23.6 billion loan from the New York Fed. As collateral, the bank pledged all its domestic assets and all its customers' securities it was allowed to use for such purposes. Altogether, the collateral was worth [$]36 billion, according to the Fed. … Around 5 a.m. Friday, the bank finally completed reconstruction of its customers' transactions from Wednesday. By 10 a.m., it had done the same for the Thursday deals. But, meanwhile, the rest of the government securities industry had begun its Friday activities, and securities and an overdraft were piling up again in the Bank of New York's account at the New York Fed. "Faced with this situation," New York Fed President Corrigan told the banking subcommittee, "at about 11:30 a.m., we temporarily stopped accepting securities transfers for the account of Bank of New York in an attempt to stabilize the situation somewhat …" The stoppage lasted only for about 90 minutes that afternoon … The Bank of New York was out of pocket about $5 million, an amount equal to about 7 percent of its earnings in the first nine months of this year, to pay interest on the money it had to borrow that Thursday. … Corrigan in his more detailed testimony sounded more notes of concern. "I believe our actions were prudent, disciplined and appropriate. In saying this, I should also confess that in some respects we were a bit lucky," he said.

unverified: That the fault was specifically a 16-bit counter overflowing at 32,768. Every source opened describes it only as a programming flaw that broke somewhere past 32,000 issues against a 36,000 design limit; none names the word size.

The exact wall-clock minute BoNY's overdraft first crossed $20 billion on 21 November 1985. Ennis and Price give 'more than $20 billion by 2:15 p.m.'; the contemporaneous Washington Post account gives only the evening figure.

Whether the 1985 episode directly caused any specific later reform (the Government Securities Act of 1986, GSCC central clearing, or Fedwire daylight-overdraft pricing from 1994). The Fed's own accounts describe a 1985 policy effort on large-dollar payment risk without attributing it to BoNY, so no causal claim is made in the prose.

The prepared statements of E. Gerald Corrigan and J. Carter Bacot to the House subcommittee on 12 December 1985 were not read in the original; they are quoted here only as reproduced in the sources above.

Sources disagree on the intraday peak: the contemporaneous Washington Post report of the 12 December 1985 testimony gives a $32 billion overdraft by Thursday evening, while Ennis and Price (2015) give 'nearly $30 billion' at 8:30 p.m. The prose uses the $32 billion figure and attributes it to the 1985 report; the discrepancy is not resolved here.

The phrase 'the electronic equivalent of patching a tire' is not a verbatim quotation. The Post puts quotation marks around "patch" but renders the tire phrase unquoted, as Berry's paraphrase of how Bacot described the fix at the 12 December 1985 hearing. Later retellings quote it; the source cited here does not, so the prose and the deck report it as description rather than as Bacot's exact words.

That the Fed's record of BoNY's reserve account was append-only in the strict sense the story's phrase “in order, never overwritten” implies. What the sources carry is the property the story rests on: Ennis and Price have the New York Fed debiting the account automatically on each delivery and stating the overdraft at named times (over $20 billion at 2:15 p.m., nearly $30 billion at 8:30 p.m.), and Lacker records that the $22.6 billion advance was sized on BoNY's own incorrect estimate of its position, leaving the further $1 billion overdraft that the Fed's books caught and BoNY's did not. The wording is the story's characterisation of that record; no source uses it.
